items.headline: Perseverance captures 360° panorama of Turquoise Bay on Mars
items.title: Perseverance’s View of ‘Turquoise Bay’
items.scifi_hook: A rover stitches 818 images into a seamless Martian panorama of a geologic wonder.
items.eli5: Perseverance used its Mastcam‑Z camera to take many photos and create a 360‑degree view of Turquoise Bay.
items.why: It expands our understanding of Mars’ geology and potential habitability.
items.text: 1 Min Read Perseverance’s View of ‘Turquoise Bay’ PIA26815 Credits: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Photojournal Navigation Science Photojournal Perseverance’s View of… Photojournal Home Photojournal Search Latest Content Galleries Feedback RSS About Description NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover used its Mastcam-Z camera to capture this 360-degree panorama of “Turquoise Bay,” a geologic area of interest in the “Margin Unit.” The 818 images used to create the natural-color panorama were captured between Oct. 5 and Oct. 16, 2023, the 933rd to 944th Martian days, or sols, of the mission. Figure A is an enhanced-color version, in which color bands were processed to improve visual contrast and accentuate color differences. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed for the agency by Caltech in Pasadena, California, built and manages operations of the Perseverance rover. Arizona State University leads the operations of the Mastcam-Z instrument, working in collaboration with Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego, on the design, fabrication, testing, and operation of the cameras, and in collaboration with the Niels Bohr Institute of the University of Copenhagen on the design, fabrication, and testing of the calibration targets. items.headline: Greenland Mines says US pact could strengthen mineral supply
items.title: Greenland Mines says US pact could strengthen mineral supply
items.scifi_hook: An allied security pact aims to lock down Greenland’s critical‑mineral resources for the West.
items.eli5: A new agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland would protect rare‑earth and precious‑metal projects from non‑allied nations.
items.why: Securing rare‑earth supply reduces reliance on rival producers and supports defense and tech industries.
items.rationale: potential boost to allied mineral supply chains
items.text: Greenland Mines (NASDAQ: GRML) says the new security agreement involving the US, Denmark and Greenland shows the territory’s importance for critical minerals, securing it and protecting its resources from non-ally countries. The rare earth and precious metals company said its Greenland projects could form part of a secure allied critical-minerals supply chain. It is also proposing a North Atlantic Critical Metals Corridor linking the territory’s resources with downstream processing and industrial infrastructure in allied countries. “Today’s announcement underscores what we have long believed: Greenland is becoming one of the most strategically important regions in the world,” Greenland Mines president Bo Møller Stensgaard said. “We believe that the same strategic importance extends to the critical minerals required for defense, advanced technology and energy security.” Stensgaard added that this new agreement will help advance a framework that strengthens security, cooperation among allies and recognizes Greenland’s importance to the future of the US and other Western countries, especially when it comes to critical minerals. The deal, announced on Sept. 18, is expected to be signed during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Greenland Mines holds two major assets on the island. items.headline: Microsoft Quantum, QOLAB Propose Higher Bar For ‘Scalable’ Logical Qubits
items.title: Microsoft Quantum, QOLAB Propose Higher Bar For ‘Scalable’ Logical Qubits
items.scifi_hook: A new framework demands error‑corrected qubits that can be replicated into thousands for real quantum advantage.
items.eli5: Microsoft and QOLAB say future quantum computers need qubits that can run long calculations with built‑in error correction, not just more raw qubits.
items.why: Clearer standards could accelerate development of fault‑tolerant quantum computers.
items.text: Insider Brief Microsoft Quantum and QOLAB proposed a framework for assessing whether logical qubits can scale into fault-tolerant systems capable of useful quantum computations. The paper says scalable logical qubits should be evaluated across reliability, scale, capability and performance, rather than through qubit counts or isolated error-rate results. The framework calls for repeated error correction, universal fault-tolerant operations, low-latency feedback and a credible route to operating hundreds or thousands of logical qubits. A framework from Microsoft Quantum and QOLAB proposes that quantum computing’s next progress reports should be judged by more than a rising count of logical qubits. The paper, posted on arXiv by Microsoft Quantum researchers Matthias Troyer and Chetan Nayak and QOLAB’s John Martinis , introduces the term “scalable logical qubit” for an error-corrected qubit that can support long computations, execute a full set of fault-tolerant operations and be replicated into systems containing hundreds or thousands of logical qubits. The proposal is ultimately aimed at a more demanding common standard for evaluating an increasingly crowded field of quantum error-correction demonstrations. The industry’s use of the term, “logical qubit,” has broadened a bit over the past few years. items.headline: Assessment of 2D Materials for Scalable Quantum Processors
items.title: Researchers Assess Two-Dimensional Materials for Scalable Quantum Hardware
items.scifi_hook: Researchers explore flat‑atom layers to turn chip factories into quantum computer factories.
items.eli5: They study ultra‑thin materials to see if regular chip plants can make large quantum chips.
items.why: It could let existing factories produce quantum computers faster.
items.text: Can established microchip manufacturing techniques deliver scalable solid-state quantum processors beyond isolated devices or small sets? Evaluating current two-dimensional material platforms, this assessment highlights a need to establish comparable performance metrics between conventional CMOS fabrication and emerging quantum technologies. Leveraging existing semiconductor infrastructure offers a pragmatic pathway towards realising practical quantum computing systems.

items.headline: New Water‑Based Method Boosts Zirconium‑Hafnium Separation Efficiency
items.title: Water-based process separates zirconium and hafnium with fivefold higher efficiency
items.scifi_hook: A water‑driven technique splits two critical metals five times more efficiently than before.
items.eli5: Scientists use water chemistry to pull apart zirconium and hafnium with far less waste.
items.why: Cleaner separation lowers costs for chips and nuclear fuel production.
items.text: Oregon State University scientists have patented a better, more environmentally friendly process for separating two metals that are critical in their pure forms for the semiconductor and atomic energy industries.
